newsitem.title: LATVIA: Baltic states restate NATO goals.
newsitem.headline: Baltic states restate NATO goals.

text.p: The Baltic states of Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania reiterated their firm desire to join NATO on Tuesday in the face of stiffening Russian opposition to their inclusion in the alliance's eastward expansion.
Russia said on Tuesday that it would reconsider its new partnership with its old Cold War foe if the Western alliance offered membership to the Baltic countries.
NATO and Russia last week reached an historic agreement aimed at ending decades of mutual hostility and suspicion.

"Lithuania was forcefully incorporated into the Soviet Union and does not consider itself to be a former republic of the Soviet Union," Lithuanian President Algirdas Brazauskas told Reuters, commenting on Russian comments that it would not tolerate any attempts to bring former Soviet republics into NATO's fold.
Lithuania and its Baltic neighbours Latvia and Estonia were annexed by Moscow in 1940 and only regained their independence in 1991.
"Our position regarding NATO membership does not change," Brazauskas added.

"It is not acceptable that the legitimate rights of the Baltic states are questioned in rhetoric coming from Russia's officials," the state secretary of the Latvian foreign ministry, Maris Riekstinsh, said.

"It is unfortunate that just a few days after an agreement in principle has been reached between Russia and NATO (that) Russia's politicians are already doubting fundamental positions therein," he said.
"Estonia's final goal is to become a full member of NATO," a spokeswoman for the Estonian foreign ministry told Reuters.
The Baltic countries view NATO's protective embrace as their only shield against a potentially hostile Russia, which has ruled them for most of the past 200 years.
NATO is expected to name new candidates to join the 16-member alliance at a summit in Madrid in July, with the Czech Republic, Poland and Hungary tipped to top the list.
Diplomats and analysts say the Baltics have almost no chance of making the first round enlargement on the grounds that Moscow would view such a move as a provocation.
Russia is particularly senstive about the Baltics, which formed its western flank during the Cold War and are still home to large Russian minorities.
